source_text: Sed enim plerique iam induxerunt animo ignoscendum esse, si quando, quae ethnici, faciunt, ne nomen blasphemetur. porro blasphemia, quae nobis omni modo deuitanda est, haec opinor est, si qui nostrum ad iustam blasphemiam ethnicum deducat aut fraude aut iniuria aut contumelia aliaue materia dignae querelae, in qua nomen merito percutitur, ut merito irascatur et dominus. ceterum si de omni blasphemia dictum est, uestra causa nomen meum blasphematur, perimus uniuersi, cum totus circus scelestis suffragiis nullo merito nomen lacessit. desinamus, et non blasphemabitur. immo blasphemetur, dum sumus in obseruatione, non in exorbitatione disciplinae, dum probamur, non dum reprobamur. o blasphemiam martyrii adfinem, quae tunc me testatur Christianum, cum propterea me detestatur! benedictio est nominis maledictio custoditae disciplinae. si hominibus, inquit, uellem placere, seruus Christi non essem. sed idem alibi iubet, omnibus placere curemus. quemadmodum ego, inquit, omnibus per omnia placeo. nimirum Saturnalia et Kalendas Ianuarias celebrans hominibus placebat? an modestia et patientia ? an grauitate, an humanitate, an integritate? proinde cum dicit, omnibus omnia factus sum, ut omnes lucrifaciam: numquid idololatris idololatres? numquid ethnicis ethnicus? numquid saecularibus saecularis? sed etsi non prohibet nos conuersari cum idololatris et adulteris et ceteris criminosis dicens, ceterum de mundo exiretis, non utique eas habenas conuersationis inmittit, ut, quoniam necesse est et conuiuere nos et commisceri cum peccatoribus, idem et compeccare possimus. ubi est commercium uitae, quod apostolus concedit, ibi ** peccare, quod nemo permittit. licet conuiuere cum ethnicis, commori non licet. conuiuamus cum omnibus; conlaetemur ex communione naturae, non superstitionis. pares anima sumus, non disciplina, compossessores mundi, non erroris. quod si nobis nullum ius est communionis in huiusmodi cum extraneis, quanto scelestius est haec inter fratres frequentare. quis hoc sustinere aut defendere potest? Iudaeis dies suos festos exprobrat spiritus sanctus. sabbata, inquit, uestra et numenias et ceremonias odit anima mea. nobis, quibus sabbata extranea sunt et numeniae et feriae a deo aliquando dilectae, Saturnalia et Ianuariae et Brumae et Matronales frequentantur, munera commeant et strenae, consonant lusus, conuiuia constrepunt. o melior fides nationum in suam sectam, quae nullam sollemnitatem Christianorum sibi uindicat! non dominicum diem, non pentecosten, etiamsi nossent, nobiscum communicassent; timerent enim, ne Christiani uiderentur. nos ne ethnici pronuntiemur, non ueremur. si quid et carni indulgendum est, habes, non dicam tuos dies tantum, sed et plures. nam ethnicis semel annuus dies quisque festus est, tibi octauo quoque die. excerpe singulas sollemnitates nationum et in ordinem exsere: pentecosten implere non poterunt.
thought_title: True blasphemy is abandoning Christian discipline, not being hated for it
orientation: Tertullian is answering Christians who think they may join pagan customs to avoid bringing the Christian name into disrepute.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed most people have already brought into their mind that it must be forgiven, if sometimes they do the things which pagans do, so that the name may not be blasphemed. Further, the blasphemy which must be avoided by us in every way is this, I think, if one of us leads a pagan to just blasphemy either by fraud or by injury or by insult or by another matter worthy of complaint, in which the name is deservedly struck, so that the Lord too is deservedly angry. But if it was said about every blasphemy, 'For your cause my name is blasphemed,' we all perish, since the whole circus with wicked votes attacks the name with no deserving. Let us stop, and it will not be blasphemed. Rather let it be blasphemed, while we are in observance, not in deviation from discipline, while we are approved, not while we are rejected. O blasphemy bordering on martyrdom, which then testifies that I am a Christian, when for that reason it detests me! The cursing of the name is a blessing of guarded discipline. 'If I wished,' he says, 'to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.' But the same man elsewhere commands, 'Let us take care to please everyone.' 'Just as I,' he says, 'please everyone in all things.' Surely he was pleasing men by celebrating the Saturnalia and the Kalends of January? Or by modesty and patience? Or by seriousness, by kindness, by integrity? Therefore when he says, 'I became all things to everyone, so that I might gain all': surely an idolater to idolaters? Surely a pagan to pagans? Surely a worldly man to worldly men? But even if he does not forbid us to associate with idolaters and adulterers and other criminals, saying, 'Otherwise you would have to go out of the world,' he certainly does not let loose such reins of association, so that, since it is necessary both to live with and to mingle with sinners, we can also sin together with them. Where there is the commerce of life, which the apostle allows, there it is a sin, which no one permits. It is allowed to live with pagans, it is not allowed to die with them. Let us live with everyone; let us rejoice together from the fellowship of nature, not of superstition. We are equals in soul, not in discipline, co-possessors of the world, not of error. But if we have no right of fellowship in things of this kind with outsiders, how much more wicked is it to frequent these things among brothers. Who can endure or defend this? The Holy Spirit reproaches the Jews for their festal days. 'Your sabbaths,' he says, 'and new moons and ceremonies my soul hates.' By us, for whom sabbaths are foreign and new moons and festivals once loved by God, the Saturnalia and the Kalends of January and the Bruma and the Matronalia are frequented, gifts go back and forth and New Year's gifts, games resound, banquets make a din. O better the faith of the nations in their own sect, which claims no solemnity of the Christians for itself! Not the Lord's day, not Pentecost, even if they knew them, would they have shared with us; for they would fear, lest they seem to be Christians. We do not fear, lest we be pronounced pagans. If anything must be indulged to the flesh, you have, I will not say your own days only, but more. For for pagans each festal day is once a year, for you every eighth day. Pick out each solemnity of the nations and set them out in order: they will not be able to fill up a Pentecost.

pass_b_english: But many have already persuaded themselves that it should be forgiven if at any time they do what pagans do, so that the name may not be blasphemed. Now the blasphemy which we must avoid in every way is, I think, this: if one of us leads a pagan to a just blasphemy by fraud or injury or insult or any other ground for legitimate complaint, in which the name is deservedly struck, so that the Lord too is deservedly angry. But if it was said of every blasphemy, 'Because of you my name is blasphemed' (Romans 2:24, citing Isaiah 52:5), we all perish, since the whole circus with its wicked acclamations attacks the name with no merit on our part. Let us stop, and it will not be blasphemed. No, let it be blasphemed, as long as we are in observance, not in deviation from discipline; as long as we are approved, not reproved. O blasphemy bordering on martyrdom, which testifies that I am a Christian at the very moment it detests me for that reason! The curse of the name is a blessing when discipline is kept.

'If I wanted to please men,' he says, 'I would not be a servant of Christ' (Galatians 1:10). But the same apostle elsewhere commands that we take care to please everyone. 'Just as I,' he says, 'please everyone in everything' (1 Corinthians 10:33). Surely he pleased men by celebrating the Saturnalia and the Kalends of January? Or by modesty and patience? By seriousness, by kindness, by integrity? Likewise when he says, 'I have become all things to all people, so that I might gain all' (1 Corinthians 9:22), was he an idolater to idolaters? A pagan to pagans? A worldly man to worldly people? But even if he does not forbid us to associate with idolaters and adulterers and other criminals, saying, 'Otherwise you would have to go out of the world' (1 Corinthians 5:10), he certainly does not let loose the reins of association to such an extent that, since it is necessary for us both to live with and mingle with sinners, we may also sin together with them. Where there is the commerce of life, which the apostle allows, there sinning together is what no one permits. It is permitted to live with pagans; it is not permitted to die with them. Let us live with everyone; let us rejoice together from the fellowship of nature, not of superstition. We are equal in soul, not in discipline; co-possessors of the world, not of error. But if we have no right of fellowship in such things with outsiders, how much more wicked is it to frequent these things among brothers. Who can endure or defend this?

The Holy Spirit reproaches the Jews for their festival days. 'Your sabbaths,' he says, 'and new moons and ceremonies my soul hates' (Isaiah 1:13-14). But we, to whom sabbaths are foreign, and new moons and festivals once loved by God, frequent the Saturnalia and the Kalends of January and the winter solstice and the Matronalia; gifts come and go, New Year's presents, games resound, banquets make a din. The faith of the pagans in their own sect is better, which claims no solemnity of the Christians for itself! They would not share with us the Lord's day or Pentecost, even if they knew them; for they would fear to seem Christians. We do not fear being pronounced pagans. If something must be indulged to the flesh, you have—I will not say only your own days—but more. For pagans each festival day comes once a year; for you every eighth day. Pick out each solemnity of the pagans and arrange them in order: they will not be able to fill up Pentecost.
